conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time today. I’m Claire Ramirez, a licensed clinical social worker who specializes in helping new mothers navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after childbirth. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a brief, well-studied questionnaire that looks at how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past week. Your answers are completely confidential; the goal is simply to understand how best to support you right now. We’ll go through ten questions together, and you can answer in your own words—no right or wrong responses. When you’re ready, we can begin.

To start: Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Honestly… I can still laugh, but it feels like I have to work harder for it. Like, when my sister sent me that silly video of her dog wearing socks, I chuckled, but it faded fast. Most of the time I’m just tired, so even when something’s funny, I don’t feel the same lightness I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I can still laugh, but it feels kind of forced—like I’m doing it because I know I should, not because it comes naturally.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to little things—like my morning coffee or when my mom brings over dinner—but the excitement feels kind of muted. It’s more “oh, that’ll be nice” instead of the bubbly feeling I used to get.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like last night when the baby wouldn’t settle for two hours, I kept thinking maybe I missed his sleepy window or I’d overstimulated him somehow. Deep down I know babies just cry, but the thought still pops in that I should’ve handled it better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… a couple of times this week I’ve caught myself just staring at the baby monitor, heart racing, sure something was wrong even though he was perfectly fine. It’s like my mind invents these scary “what-ifs” out of nowhere, and I can’t shake the tightness in my chest until I go check on him.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Um… maybe once or twice. Nothing full-blown, but I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly feel this wave of “something bad is about to happen.” My chest gets tight, breathing feels shallow, and for a minute I think I might pass out. It passes if I pace the hallway or do that slow-breathing thing the nurse showed me, but it’s unsettling while it lasts.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… especially mid-afternoon when the baby’s had a short nap and the dishes are piled up. I’ll look around and just feel this weight—like there’s no way I’ll get through the feedings, the laundry, the texts I haven’t answered. I usually still manage, but I end up snapping at my partner or crying in the shower because everything feels like too much.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I’m tired all the time, but when I finally lie down my mind keeps spinning—did I sanitize the pump parts, is the baby breathing, what if I sleep through his cry? So I toss and turn for an hour or two, and even when I do drop off I wake up at every little sound. It’s more worry than sadness keeping me awake.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some days, but it comes and goes. Like yesterday evening, once the baby was finally down, I just sat on the couch and felt this heavy, weepy feeling for maybe half an hour. It’s not there every moment—sometimes I’m okay and even enjoy little things—but yes, I’ve definitely had spells of feeling low and tearful.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really “so unhappy” that I cry—at least not most days. I’ve teared up a couple of times when I’m really worn out, like yesterday when I spilled the pumped milk, but it’s not an everyday thing and it passes pretty quickly once I blow my nose and take a breath.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel overwhelmed or tired, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Clinical Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wk postpartum, first live birth, partner support present.

Symptoms endorsed:
- Dysthymic mood with intermittent tearfulness (Q8)
- Marked anhedonia / muted enjoyment (Q1, Q2)
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)
- Recurrent, intrusive “what-if” worries, monitor-checking, nocturnal rumination (Q4, Q7)
- Two sub-threshold panic-like episodes (tight chest, shallow breathing, no acute trigger) (Q5)
- Frequent overwhelm / emotional lability, especially afternoons; functional tasks still completed (Q6)
- Mild, situational crying spells, quickly remitting (Q9)
- No self-harm ideation (Q10)

Patterns / risk indicators:
- Persistent low mood and reduced pleasure ≥ 2 wk
- Anxiety symptoms (GAD & panic spectrum) co-occurring with low mood
- Sleep disruption secondary to intrusive worries rather than infant needs alone
- No safety concerns (denies suicidal/harm thoughts)

Screening impression:
Elevated scores consistent with probable postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety features; further evaluation with EPDS/PHQ-9/GAD-7 and clinical interview warranted. Safety risk currently low; continue monitoring.
